skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: On the invented island of Tessarin, fishers have long timed their voyages by the flowering of a small purple shrub called the saltbell. When the shrub blooms, the sea along the east coast warms enough for sardines to arrive in the shallows. Younger fishers now rely on temperature gauges, but many of them admit that the shrub is still the more dependable signal.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Temperature gauges are too inaccurate to be used by fishers on Tessarin.
Fishers on Tessarin have traditionally used the blooming of the saltbell to judge when sardines will arrive.
Sardines on Tessarin prefer cold water and avoid the east coast.
The saltbell shrub grows only where the sea is warm.
why: The passage centres on fishers using the saltbell's bloom as a sign that sardines are coming, so B is right. A overstates the passage, which says only that many fishers find the shrub more dependable, and C reverses the point about warming water.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: The village of Pell Harbor keeps time with a clock powered by rainwater. Rain collects in a tank on the roof, and as the tank fills, its growing weight slowly lowers a chain that turns the clock's gears. When the tank is full, a valve opens and drains the water, and a caretaker winches the chain back up so that the cycle can begin again.
stem: According to the text, what causes the chain in the Pell Harbor clock to lower?
opts: The caretaker winding the chain by hand
The valve opening at the bottom of the tank
The increasing weight of the water collecting in the roof tank
The turning of the clock's gears
why: The text says the tank's growing weight lowers the chain, so C is correct. The caretaker (A) winches the chain back up, and the valve (B) only drains the tank.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Composer Ilya Brandt wrote his Winter Suite for a small-town brass band that had only nine members. Rather than treat the band's size as a handicap, he gave each player a part that allowed that musician to stand out, with short solos passed from one instrument to the next. Critics who heard the first performance praised the suite's clarity, saying that every line could be heard.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Brandt turned the small size of the band into a strength by giving each player a distinct part.
Brandt wished that his band had more members so that it could play louder.
Critics disliked the Winter Suite because its solos were too short.
Brandt wrote the Winter Suite after several critics urged him to do so.
why: The passage says Brandt did not treat the band's size as a handicap and instead wrote solo parts for each player, so A is right. B contradicts that approach, and C and D invent critic reactions the text does not report.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Octopuses are unusual in having three hearts. Two of them pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen, while the third circulates that blood to the rest of the body. When an octopus swims, the third heart briefly stops beating, which may explain why these animals tend to crawl along the seabed rather than swim long distances.
stem: According to the text, what is the function of the octopus's third heart?
opts: It pumps blood through the gills.
It keeps beating only while the octopus swims.
It allows the octopus to hold its breath.
It circulates oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body.
why: The text states that the third heart circulates blood to the rest of the body, so D is correct. The two other hearts, not the third, pump blood through the gills (A), and the third heart actually stops when the octopus swims (B).

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: A student named Priya hypothesizes that houseplants grow taller on east-facing windowsills than on north-facing ones because the east-facing sills receive more hours of direct sunlight. She plans to place identical seedlings on both kinds of sill, give them the same water and soil, and measure their heights after eight weeks.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Priya's hypothesis?
opts: The seedlings on the north-facing sills were watered more often than those on the east-facing sills.
The seedlings on the east-facing sills received more hours of direct sunlight and were taller on average after eight weeks.
The seedlings on both kinds of sill were about the same height after eight weeks.
The seedlings on the north-facing sills grew more leaves than those on the east-facing sills.
why: B shows both the extra sunlight and the greater height that Priya's hypothesis predicts. A would be a flaw in the experiment, C would contradict the hypothesis, and D concerns leaves, not height.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: The Karvel Plateau is dry and almost treeless, yet it supports a surprising number of grazing animals. Seasonal rains are brief, but for about six weeks they turn the grasses green, and herds travel hundreds of kilometres to feed during that window. Once the grass withers, the animals scatter to the valleys below.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: The valleys below the Karvel Plateau are greener than the plateau itself.
Grazing animals prefer dry land because it has fewer predators.
Although the Karvel Plateau is dry, brief seasonal rains let it support large grazing herds for part of the year.
Trees cannot grow on the Karvel Plateau because the herds eat their seedlings.
why: The passage explains that short rains briefly green the plateau and draw herds, which C captures. A is only a side detail, and B and D give causes the text never mentions.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: In the market town of Dunmere, traders once settled debts with salt rather than coins. A merchant would weigh out the salt and hand it over, and the seller would store it until it was needed to preserve meat in winter. Coins were rare in the town because the nearest mint was three weeks' journey away.
stem: According to the text, why were coins rare in Dunmere?
opts: The nearest mint was a long journey from the town.
Merchants refused to accept payment in metal.
Salt was too heavy to exchange for coins.
Sellers needed coins to preserve meat in winter.
why: The last sentence gives the reason: the mint was three weeks away. The other options misuse details; salt, not coins, was used to preserve meat.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Dr. Hana Lindqvist asked sixty volunteers to memorize a list of twenty words. Half of the volunteers took a ten-minute walk before studying, and the other half sat quietly. When tested an hour later, the walkers remembered an average of fourteen words, while the sitters remembered an average of eleven. Lindqvist cautioned that the study was small but called the difference worth investigating further.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Volunteers who sat quietly were unable to memorize any words.
Lindqvist believes that walking is harmful to memory.
A small study found that volunteers who walked before studying remembered more words than those who sat.
Memorizing twenty words is too difficult for most volunteers.
why: C reports the study's design and result accurately, including the caution about its size. A overstates (the sitters recalled eleven words on average), and B and D contradict or ignore the text.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Ecologist Tomas Reyes proposes that the pale colour of the glassfin minnow helps it avoid predators in the sandy shallows of Lake Orvane. According to his idea, a pale fish is harder for hunting birds and larger fish to see against a light sandy bottom than a dark fish would be.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Reyes's proposal?
opts: Glassfin minnows living over sandy bottoms are, on average, paler in winter than in summer.
In tanks with sandy bottoms, predatory fish caught pale minnows less often than they caught dark minnows.
The predators in Lake Orvane hunt mainly by smell rather than by sight.
Pale minnows are more common in the deeper parts of the lake than in the shallows.
why: B directly shows that pale colour reduces capture on a sandy bottom. C would weaken the idea because it removes the role of sight, and A and D describe where or when minnows are pale without showing any link to survival.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Economist Lena Park argues that the opening of a new tram line in March caused sales at shops on Quarry Street to rise 12 percent last year. She points out that the tram stops directly in front of the street's main entrance and that sales rose in the months after the line opened.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Park's argument?
opts: The tram line carried about four thousand riders per day last year.
Several shops on Quarry Street opened after March of last year.
Shops on other streets with no access to the tram line also saw their sales rise by about 12 percent.
Sales on Quarry Street had been flat in the years before the tram line opened.
why: If shops far from the tram saw the same rise, something other than the tram probably explains it, so C weakens the causal claim. A and D are consistent with Park's argument, and B is too vague to undermine it.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Glassblowers in the invented city of Veshti once guarded their furnace recipes jealously, passing them on only to apprentices. After a flood destroyed the guild hall in 1840, however, the surviving members began writing the recipes down so that they could not be lost again. Historians credit this change with the later spread of Veshti glass across the region.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: A disaster led Veshti glassblowers to record formerly secret recipes, which helped their glass reach new markets.
A flood destroyed every furnace in Veshti and ended the city's glassmaking.
Veshti apprentices objected to having the recipes written down.
Historians disagree about whether the flood affected Veshti glass.
why: A links the flood, the written recipes and the later spread of Veshti glass, which is the passage's chain of events. B overstates the damage (only the guild hall is mentioned), and C and D add claims the text does not make.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Astronomers at the invented Kellan Observatory found that a faint dwarf star named Ormund 7 dims by about 20 percent every nine days. The pattern led the team to suspect that a planet was crossing the star's face. To test the idea, they checked whether the dimming lasted the same length of time in each cycle, as a planet's steady passage would predict. It did.
stem: According to the text, what did the astronomers do to test their suspicion that a planet was crossing the star?
opts: They measured the mass of Ormund 7.
They looked for times when the star grew brighter than usual.
They compared Ormund 7 with other faint dwarf stars.
They checked whether the dimming lasted equally long in each cycle.
why: The text says the team checked whether each dimming lasted the same length of time, which is D. The other options describe procedures that are never mentioned.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: A student is writing about The Lantern Keeper, an invented novel, and wants to show that its main character, Joss, is cautious by nature. She notes that Joss lives beside a frozen creek that he must cross each morning to reach the village school, and that the other children cross it quickly and carelessly.
stem: Which quotation from the novel would most effectively illustrate the student's claim?
opts: Joss grinned at the others and leapt across the creek before anyone could stop him.
Before crossing the frozen creek, Joss tested the ice with a stick three times, and then he walked the long way round anyway.
Joss crossed the creek each morning, humming a tune his grandmother had taught him.
The other children laughed as they raced across the ice, calling for Joss to hurry.
why: B shows repeated checking and a decision to avoid the risk, which is what cautious means. A shows the opposite, and C and D mention the crossing without revealing how careful Joss is.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: A start-up in Cobalt Bay has developed a battery that charges in four minutes but wears out after about three hundred charges, roughly a year of daily use. Engineers say that for delivery vans, which are recharged overnight, the speed offers little advantage while the short life raises costs. For taxi drivers, who lose income whenever a car sits charging, the speed could outweigh the short life.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Delivery vans should never use batteries that charge quickly.
The Cobalt Bay battery is the first battery to charge in under five minutes.
The value of the battery depends on whether fast charging matters more to a user than a long battery life.
Taxi drivers earn more money than delivery drivers do.
why: The passage contrasts two kinds of users to show that the battery's worth depends on how each weighs charging speed against lifespan, as C says. A is too absolute, and B and D bring in claims the passage does not support.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Coach Ines Falk of the invented Harrowgate Rowing Club asked her crews to row in complete silence for the first ten minutes of each practice. She hypothesizes that the crews' timing improved because the rowers listened more closely to the sound of the oars entering the water and used that sound to keep together.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Falk's hypothesis?
opts: Rowers who wore earplugs that blocked the sound of the oars kept worse time than rowers without earplugs, even when no one spoke.
Rowers said that they felt more rested after practices that began in silence.
Crews that talked during warm-up finished races faster than crews that stayed silent.
Most rowers at the club said that they preferred silent practices to noisy ones.
why: Falk's claim concerns listening to oar sounds; A shows that removing those sounds hurts timing, which supports the mechanism. C would work against her, and B and D concern feelings rather than timing.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Conservators examining paintings by the invented artist Odalys Weir noticed that the blue skies in works hung in a sunlit gallery had faded to grey, while the skies in works kept in a dim storage room remained vivid. Weir mixed her blue from a mineral pigment, and the conservators suspect that long exposure to light slowly breaks down the colour of that mineral.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Weir painted most of her skies in grey.
Conservators have proved that all mineral pigments fade.
Weir's paintings are worth more when they are kept in storage.
Conservators suspect that light fades the mineral blue Weir used, based on differences between displayed and stored paintings.
why: D reports the observation and the cautious explanation the conservators offer. A and C are not supported, and B overstates a suspicion about one pigment into a proof about all pigments.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Psychologist Anil Rao suggests that people recall unfinished tasks better than finished ones because an unfinished task stays active in the mind. In his study, sixty volunteers solved puzzles, and half of them were interrupted before they could finish. Later, the volunteers recalled the interrupted puzzles more readily than the completed ones.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Rao's explanation of the result?
opts: Volunteers rated the puzzles as equally enjoyable whether or not they were interrupted.
The puzzles that were interrupted were also the most unusual and difficult ones, and unusual puzzles tend to be remembered well.
Volunteers who finished their puzzles took an average of eleven minutes to do so.
Several volunteers said that they had solved similar puzzles before.
why: B offers a different reason, the puzzles' unusualness, for the better recall, so interruption may not be the cause. A, C and D do not offer a competing explanation for the difference in recall.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: When the Almora olive cooperative began pooling its members' olives for pressing, each family's cost per litre of oil fell by a third, because one large press runs more efficiently than many small ones. The families also lost the ability to sell oil under their own labels, since all of it was now bottled together. Several members complained about that loss.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: The Almora cooperative closed after its members complained.
Large presses always produce better oil than small presses.
Pooling olives made oil production cheaper for the cooperative's families but ended their ability to sell under separate labels.
Olive growers in Almora prefer to bottle oil under their own names.
why: The text names one gain (lower cost) and one loss (separate labels), as C does. A is not stated, B overgeneralizes about presses, and D generalizes from the complaints of several members.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Archivist Selma Quist studied the ledgers of the invented Brightwater mill and found that the cash wages recorded for women were consistently lower than those recorded for men doing the same tasks. Some scholars take this as proof that the owners valued women's work less. Quist cautions that the ledgers list only cash; women, she notes, were frequently paid partly in grain and housing, which the ledgers do not record.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: Quist suggests that the lower cash wages for women in the ledgers may not show the full extent of their pay.
Quist proves that the mill paid women more than it paid men.
Quist argues that the ledgers are unreliable and should be ignored.
Quist agrees with the scholars that the owners valued women's work less.
why: Quist warns that cash alone may understate women's pay, so A is correct. B overstates her caution into a proof, C goes too far because she questions the interpretation rather than the ledgers, and D reverses her stance.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Biologist Mireille Tan observed that Calder geckos, which are active only at night, have eyes about 30 percent larger relative to body size than those of related geckos that are active by day. She concludes that the Calder gecko's large eyes evolved to help it see in dim light.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Tan's conclusion?
opts: Several other night-active animals in the same habitat also have unusually large eyes.
Calder geckos living in the dimmest valleys have larger eyes than Calder geckos living in brighter valleys.
Day-active geckos are more numerous than night-active geckos in the region.
The day-active ancestors of the Calder gecko, which lived in bright, open habitats, already had eyes of the same large size.
why: If the large eyes were already present in day-active ancestors, they cannot have evolved for night vision, so D undercuts Tan's claim. A and B fit her conclusion, and C does not bear on why the eyes are large.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Wen stood at the ferry rail with his father's watch heavy in his coat pocket. He had meant to sell it in the city to pay his first term's fees, and he had rehearsed the sale all week: the shrug, the casual price. Now, as the far shore thickened into streets, he found his thumb moving over the watch's cracked glass again and again, as if smoothing it might undo the crack.
stem: Which choice best describes the main idea of the text?
opts: Wen is angry with his father for leaving him the watch.
Wen plans to sell the watch but is feeling a reluctance that he has not openly admitted.
Wen has decided to keep the watch and pay his fees another way.
Wen is nervous about starting his first term at school.
why: His rehearsed plan to sell the watch and his repeated stroking of its cracked glass together suggest unspoken reluctance, as B states. C goes beyond the text because no decision is made, and A and D are not supported by anything in the scene.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: A music student claims that the invented composer Hedda Voss became more interested in silence as her career went on. To support the claim, the student plans to point to a measurable change in how Voss's later symphonies treat moments in which the orchestra does not play, as opposed to how loudly or softly the orchestra plays.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most effectively support the student's claim?
opts: Voss's later symphonies contain more passages marked as quiet than her early symphonies do.
Voss's later symphonies were, on average, shorter than her early symphonies.
The rests in Voss's symphonies lengthened from an average of two beats in her early works to an average of seven beats in her late works.
Critics generally preferred Voss's early symphonies to her late ones.
why: The claim concerns silence, meaning moments when the orchestra does not play, and longer rests measure exactly that. A is a close distractor because quiet music is not the same as no music, and B and D do not address silence.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Astronomers tracking the comet Halvard-Ito noticed that it brightened sharply as it neared the Sun and then dimmed just as sharply, well before it reached its closest point. One explanation is that the comet vented gas and dust in a burst that faded as its supply ran low. Another is that the comet broke apart, and its fragments, individually faint, spread out. Images taken during the dimming showed a single compact nucleus with no sign of debris.
stem: Based on the text, what do the images taken during the dimming suggest?
opts: The dimming is better explained by a fading burst of venting than by the comet breaking apart.
The comet broke apart into fragments too faint to see.
The comet had already passed its closest point to the Sun.
Neither explanation for the dimming is possible.
why: A single intact nucleus and no debris count against the breakup explanation and leave the venting explanation standing, so A is right. B contradicts the images, C contradicts the text's statement that the dimming came well before the closest point, and D overstates because the venting explanation survives.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: Economist Calla Ferreira studied farmers in the invented Sorrel Valley who adopted drip irrigation, and she found that their water use fell by 35 percent. She argues that the saving came from the technology itself. A critic replies that the adopters were mostly farmers who had earlier completed a water-management training programme, and that the training, not the equipment, may explain the saving.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Ferreira's argument over the critic's?
opts: The farmers who adopted drip irrigation were wealthier on average than those who did not.
Farmers who had completed the training were already using less water than other farmers before drip irrigation was introduced.
Drip irrigation systems cost more to install than the older systems they replaced.
Among farmers who had all completed the training, those who installed drip irrigation cut their water use by about 33 percent, while those who did not changed little.
why: D holds the training constant and still finds a large saving only among those who installed drip irrigation, which isolates the technology. B would favor the critic, and A and C do not help separate the effect of the equipment from that of the training.

skill: Central Ideas and Details, and Command of Evidence (textual)
passage: When the Skerrin Point lighthouse was automated, its keeper's logbook came to an end. The loss mattered less for the light than for the record: for ninety years, keepers had noted fog, birds and passing ships in a continuous hand, and no instrument installed since has logged the birds. Researchers now reconstruct bird migrations from the old entries, even though the keepers never meant them as scientific data.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
opts: The keepers' logbooks, though never meant as science, now serve as a valuable record that automation did not carry on.
Automation made the Skerrin Point light less reliable than it had been under its keepers.
Researchers criticize the keepers for recording birds in a careless way.
Modern instruments record birds more accurately than the keepers did.
why: The passage stresses that the old entries are now useful to researchers and that automation ended the record, which A captures. B, C and D invent claims about reliability, carelessness and accuracy that the text never makes.

passage: Student researcher Lena Oduya grew sunflower seedlings for four weeks under three conditions and then measured average plant height. Plants given no fertilizer averaged 31 centimeters. Plants given Mix A averaged 42 centimeters. Plants given Mix B averaged 55 centimeters. Lena claims that Mix B was the most effective of the three conditions for growing tall sunflowers.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support Lena's claim?
opts: Mix B plants averaged 55 centimeters, taller than the 42 centimeters of Mix A plants and the 31 centimeters of unfertilized plants.
Mix A plants averaged 42 centimeters, which is 11 centimeters taller than the unfertilized plants.
Unfertilized plants averaged 31 centimeters after four weeks of growth.
Plants given either Mix A or Mix B averaged more than 40 centimeters.
why: Choice A compares Mix B with both other conditions, so it shows Mix B was tallest. Choice D is true but treats the two mixes together and does not show that B beat A.

passage: The village of Tarn Hollow has two bakeries. Last winter, one of them closed for repairs, and the other sold out of bread by 9 a.m. every day. When the first bakery reopened in spring, the second bakery's bread stayed on the shelves until noon. The earlier sell-outs were most likely caused by ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: a sudden rise in the price of flour in the village
a decline in the quality of the second bakery's bread
customers who had no other place to buy bread while the first bakery was closed
a decision by the second bakery to open later in the morning
why: Bread lasted longer once a second source of bread returned, so the extra buyers during the closure explain the sell-outs. Choice B is wrong because lower quality would not make bread sell out faster.

passage: A ferry company counted passengers on three days of one week. On Monday the ferry carried 120 passengers. On Wednesday it carried 95 passengers. On Saturday it carried 210 passengers. A manager says that Saturday is the busiest of these three days.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the manager's statement?
opts: On Wednesday the ferry carried 95 passengers, which was fewer than the 120 it carried on Monday.
On Saturday the ferry carried 210 passengers, nearly double Monday's 120 and more than double Wednesday's 95.
On Monday and Wednesday together, the ferry carried a total of 215 passengers.
The number of passengers on the ferry varied from one day to another during the week.
why: Choice B compares Saturday's count directly with both other days. Choice A compares only Monday and Wednesday, which says nothing about Saturday.

passage: On Kessel Island, a certain beetle comes in two colors, green and brown. Brown beetles are common on the dry brown hillsides, while green beetles are common in the wet green meadows. A biologist proposes that hunting birds mostly catch beetles that stand out against their background. If the biologist is right, a brown beetle placed in a green meadow would most likely be ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: harder for birds to see than the green beetles around it
just as likely to survive as a brown beetle on a hillside
invisible to birds until it moves to a hillside
easier for birds to spot, and so more likely to be caught, than the green beetles around it
why: If birds catch beetles that contrast with their surroundings, a brown beetle on green would stand out. Choice A reverses this idea.

passage: A town library recorded the number of visits in three months of the same year: 340 visits in January, 410 visits in February, and 520 visits in March. The librarian says that library visits rose in every one of these months compared with the month before.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the librarian's statement?
opts: The library was open for business in January, February, and March.
Visits increased from 340 in January to 410 in February and then to 520 in March.
March was the busiest of the three months, with 520 visits.
February had more visits than January, with 410 compared with 340.
why: Choice B gives all three figures in order, so it shows a rise at each step. Choice D shows only the first rise and says nothing about March.

passage: Ivo practiced the violin for 20 minutes a day during his first month of lessons and learned to play two songs. In his second month he practiced for 60 minutes a day and learned to play eight songs. Ivo's results suggest that the amount of time he spent practicing ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: affected how quickly he learned new songs
had no effect on the number of songs he learned
mattered less than the type of violin he used
was unrelated to how much he enjoyed the lessons
why: More daily practice went with more songs learned, so practice time likely affected his speed. Choices C and D bring in ideas the text never mentions.

passage: A weather station in a coastal town recorded the monthly rainfall over one summer. In June, 12 millimeters of rain fell. In July, 8 millimeters fell. In August, 3 millimeters fell. A resident claims that the rainfall in the town decreased steadily as the summer went on.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the resident's claim?
opts: The weather station recorded rainfall in June, July, and August.
The town received 12 millimeters of rain in June, more than in any later month.
August was the driest of the three months, with only 3 millimeters of rain.
Rainfall fell from 12 millimeters in June to 8 millimeters in July and then to 3 millimeters in August.
why: Choice D shows a drop from each month to the next, which is what steady decrease means. Choices B and C each show only one comparison.

passage: A student placed a bean seedling in a box with a small hole in one side. After a week, the stem had bent toward the hole. She then moved the hole to the opposite side of the box, and over the next week the stem slowly bent in that new direction. These results suggest that the direction in which the seedling grows is influenced by ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: the age of the seedling at the start of the test
the amount of water in the soil
the position of the opening that lets light into the box
the thickness of the walls of the box
why: The stem followed the hole when it moved, and the hole is where light enters. The age and water are never changed, so they cannot explain the change in direction.

passage: A warehouse tested three picking robots for one hour each. Model X picked 48 items and made 6 errors. Model Y picked 60 items and made 15 errors. Model Z picked 36 items and made 1 error. An engineer concludes that Model Y was the fastest of the three robots but also the least accurate.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the engineer's conclusion?
opts: Model Y picked 60 items, more than Model X's 48 or Model Z's 36, but made 15 errors, more than Model X's 6 or Model Z's 1.
Model Z made only 1 error, but it picked just 36 items in the hour.
Model X picked 48 items and made 6 errors, a middle result on both measures.
Model Y made 15 errors, which is more than the 6 errors made by Model X.
why: Choice A covers both parts of the conclusion, speed and errors, against both other models. Choice D covers only errors and only one comparison.

passage: A historian studied the port ledgers of the town of Dunmere. Before a canal opened upriver in 1832, the ledgers show about 40 trading ships arriving each year. In the years after the canal opened, they show only about 15 arrivals a year. Over the same period, the records of the inland market town of Ashby show steadily growing trade. These records suggest that the canal most likely ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: caused Dunmere to build a larger number of ships
moved trade away from the port of Dunmere and toward inland towns such as Ashby
was built because Dunmere's port was already empty of ships
had little effect on where merchants chose to trade
why: Port arrivals fell after the canal opened while an inland town's trade grew, which fits trade shifting inland. Choice C reverses the order of events given in the ledgers.

passage: A cafe owner tested two prices for a latte. In one week, at a price of $4 per cup, the cafe sold 500 lattes. In the next week, at a price of $5 per cup, it sold 380 lattes. The owner claims that raising the price lowered the cafe's total income from lattes even though each cup earned more.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the owner's claim?
opts: At the price of $5, the cafe sold fewer lattes than it did at the price of $4.
In the second week, the cafe earned $5 for each latte that it sold.
At $4 per cup the cafe took in $2,000 from lattes in a week, but at $5 per cup it took in only $1,900.
The cafe sold 120 fewer lattes in the second week than in the first week, so its income grew.
why: Choice C converts the figures into weekly totals ($4 x 500 and $5 x 380), which is what the claim is about. Choice A is true but says nothing about total income.

passage: Marisol told everyone at work that she hated surprises. Yet when her coworkers hid behind a door on her birthday and jumped out, she laughed so hard that she cried and asked them to do it again next year. Her reaction suggests that her statement about hating surprises was probably ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: a sign that she dislikes the people she works with
a response to an unpleasant party she had attended in the past
a carefully thought-out and consistent opinion
more of an assumption about herself than a true feeling
why: Her delighted reaction contradicts her statement, so the statement was likely not a true preference. Choice A has no support, since she asked them to repeat the surprise.

passage: A sprinter ran the 100-meter dash in four races. Her times were 12.4 seconds in the first race, 12.1 seconds in the second, 11.9 seconds in the third, and 11.8 seconds in the fourth. Her coach says that the sprinter improved in every race, but that each improvement was smaller than the one before it.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the coach's statement?
opts: Her fastest time was 11.8 seconds, which she ran in the fourth race.
Her time dropped by 0.3 second from the first race to the second, by 0.2 second from the second to the third, and by 0.1 second from the third to the fourth.
Her slowest time was 12.4 seconds, which she ran in the first race.
She ran 12.4 seconds in the first race and 12.1 seconds in the second race.
why: Choice B gives all three gaps, and they shrink from 0.3 to 0.2 to 0.1. Choices A and C name only the endpoints, which cannot show how each step compares with the next.

passage: Dr. Ansel Brekke asked 60 volunteers to learn a list of words in the morning. Afterward, half of the volunteers rested quietly for 30 minutes, and the other half read a gripping novel for 30 minutes. Later in the day, the volunteers who had rested recalled more words than those who had read. Brekke concluded that reading the novel most likely lowered recall because it ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: was more tiring than resting, and tiredness is known to cause forgetting
gave the volunteers extra practice with the word list
kept the volunteers' attention occupied when they could have been settling the word list in memory
had no connection to the list of words at all
why: Quiet rest gave the new words time to settle, while the novel demanded attention. Choice B is wrong because it would predict better recall for the readers, not worse.

passage: A geographer measured three lakes. Lake Orin has a surface area of 12 square kilometers and a depth of 40 meters. Lake Pell has a surface area of 30 square kilometers and a depth of 15 meters. Lake Quay has a surface area of 5 square kilometers and a depth of 90 meters. The geographer claims that a lake with a larger surface area is not necessarily a deeper lake.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the geographer's claim?
opts: Lake Pell has the largest area, 30 square kilometers, but a depth of only 15 meters, while Lake Quay has the smallest area, 5 square kilometers, but the greatest depth, 90 meters.
Lake Orin has a surface area of 12 square kilometers and a depth of 40 meters.
Lake Quay, at 90 meters, is deeper than Lake Orin, at 40 meters.
Lake Pell covers a larger area than Lake Orin, 30 square kilometers compared with 12.
why: Choice A pairs the largest area with a shallow depth and the smallest area with the greatest depth, which shows size does not predict depth. Choice D compares only area.

passage: Engineers at Brightwater Labs tested two phone batteries. At 25 degrees Celsius, both Battery A and Battery B lasted about 10 hours. At minus 10 degrees Celsius, Battery A lasted 9 hours, but Battery B lasted only 4 hours. A company that makes phones for winter hikers must choose between the two batteries. Based on the tests, the company should most likely choose ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: Battery B, because it matches Battery A in warm conditions
either battery, because both lasted 10 hours at 25 degrees Celsius
Battery B, because 4 hours is long enough for any hike
Battery A, because its running time dropped only slightly in the cold
why: Hikers use phones in the cold, where Battery A kept most of its running time and Battery B lost more than half. Choices A and B rely on the warm result, which is irrelevant to winter use.

passage: A concert hall tracked its season-ticket sales over four years. It sold 800 season tickets in 2021, 950 in 2022, 1,100 in 2023, and 1,030 in 2024. The hall's director says that after two consecutive years of growth, sales fell slightly in the most recent year.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the director's statement?
opts: Sales were highest in 2023, when the hall sold 1,100 season tickets.
Sales in 2024, at 1,030 tickets, were higher than sales in 2021, at 800 tickets.
Sales rose from 800 in 2021 to 950 in 2022 and 1,100 in 2023 before dipping to 1,030 in 2024.
Sales rose steadily from 800 tickets in 2021 to 1,030 tickets in 2024.
why: Choice C shows two increases followed by a small drop. Choice D claims steady growth through 2024, which the 2023 and 2024 figures contradict.

passage: On the island of Perrin, a farmers' cooperative sets one price for all mangoes. After a storm destroyed half of the harvest, the cooperative did not raise the price, and the mangoes sold out within an hour every morning. If the cooperative had raised the price, some shoppers would probably have ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: bought more mangoes to take advantage of the high price
decided that the mangoes cost too much and bought fewer, which would have made the supply last longer
been unable to tell that a storm had damaged the harvest
stopped caring about the price of other fruit
why: A higher price tends to reduce how much people buy, so the limited supply would have lasted longer. Choice A is unlikely, since shoppers rarely buy more because a price has gone up.

passage: Ecologists counted bird species in four forest plots. Plot 1, which has never been logged, held 42 species. Plot 2, which was selectively logged ten years ago, held 38 species. Plot 3, which was logged two years ago, held 24 species. Plot 4, which was cleared and replanted with a single type of tree, held 9 species. One ecologist claims that bird diversity in a selectively logged forest nearly recovers within about ten years.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the ecologist's claim?
opts: Plot 2, logged ten years ago, held 38 species, close to the 42 in unlogged Plot 1 and far above the 24 in Plot 3, logged two years ago.
Plot 3, logged two years ago, held 24 species, far fewer than the 42 species in Plot 1.
Plot 4 held only 9 species, the fewest of any plot.
Plot 2 held 38 species, more than the 24 in Plot 3 and the 9 in Plot 4.
why: Choice A compares the ten-year-old plot with the unlogged plot, which is what 'nearly recovers' requires, and with the recent plot. Choice D shows Plot 2 is richer than two other plots but does not show it is near the unlogged level.

passage: For decades, the lighthouse keeper Orsolya Venn filled her logbook with weather readings and lists of passing ships, and she never wrote a word about herself. After she retired, her niece found one entry, written in tiny letters in a margin on a stormy night: 'Counted forty-one ships. Missed the forty-second.' Reading it, the niece wondered whether Venn's habitually impersonal log ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: proved that Venn had disliked her work from the start
showed that the weather readings had been inaccurate throughout
was evidence that Venn resented her niece's visits
may have concealed strong personal feelings about the ships she watched over
why: The tiny note shows Venn minded missing a ship, so her plain style may have hidden what she felt. Choice A goes too far, because one regretful note does not prove she disliked the work.

passage: A bakery chain keeps records for three branches. Branch A served 2,400 customers in a month, and customers there spent an average of $6 each. Branch B served 1,500 customers, who spent an average of $11 each. Branch C served 3,000 customers, who spent an average of $4 each. An analyst claims that the branch serving the fewest customers took in the most money.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the analyst's claim?
opts: Branch C served the most customers, 3,000, but had the lowest average spending, $4.
Branch A served 2,400 customers who each spent an average of $6.
Branch B served 1,500 customers, fewer than A or C, yet its average spending of $11 meant $16,500 in total, more than A's $14,400 or C's $12,000.
Branch B had the highest average spending per customer of the three branches, at $11.
why: Choice C multiplies customers by spending for each branch and shows the smallest branch earning the most. Choice D gives the highest average spend but does not show total takings.

passage: Astronomer Dr. Imelda Caro studies a faint star whose brightness dips by 1 percent every 9 days, with each dip lasting about three hours. A planet crossing in front of the star could cause such a dip. Dark spots on the star's surface could also cause dips as they rotate into view, but spots usually shift, grow, and fade, so their dips rarely repeat on an exact schedule with an identical length. Since the dips do repeat with an identical schedule and length, Caro reasons that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: the star must be dimmer than most other stars of its kind
an orbiting planet is a more likely cause of the dips than star spots are
star spots can be ruled out with complete certainty as the cause
the star must rotate exactly once every nine days
why: Regular, identical dips fit a planet better than changing spots, so the planet is the more likely cause. Choice C overreaches: the evidence makes spots unlikely, not impossible.

passage: A psychologist asked students to rate their focus from 1 to 10 after studying in four settings. Students studying in a quiet library (30 students) averaged 7.8. Students studying in a cafe (28 students) averaged 6.9. Students studying at home with music playing (32 students) averaged 5.1. Students studying at home without music (29 students) averaged 7.2. The psychologist claims that background music lowered students' focus when the location was kept the same.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the psychologist's claim?
opts: Students in the quiet library gave the highest focus rating of the four groups, 7.8.
Students in the cafe rated their focus lower, at 6.9, than students in the library, at 7.8.
Students studying at home with music gave the lowest focus rating of the four groups, 5.1.
Students studying at home with music averaged 5.1, compared with 7.2 for students studying at home without music.
why: Choice D compares two groups in the same location that differ only in music. Choice C names the lowest group, but without a same-location comparison it could reflect something other than music.

passage: The earliest bell-tower inspection recorded in the town of Halden dates from 1604. Later reports mention repairs to the tower every 20 to 30 years, but no report between 1650 and 1710 mentions the tower at all. Historian Piet Rennard points out that the town's other civic records for those same years are also missing, because the town hall burned down in 1711. Rennard therefore cautions that the lack of tower reports from 1650 to 1710 ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
opts: does not by itself show that the tower went without repairs during those years
proves that the tower was neglected for sixty years
confirms that the fire of 1711 began at the tower
shows that the town stopped appointing inspectors after 1650
why: Since all civic records from those years are gone, missing tower reports cannot show that no repairs happened. Choice B treats missing records as proof of neglect, which the fire explanation undercuts.

passage: A technology team tested three ways of compressing the same 100-megabyte video. Method P produced a 40-megabyte file in 2 minutes, with a quality score of 92 out of 100. Method Q produced a 25-megabyte file in 8 minutes, with a quality score of 90. Method R produced a 22-megabyte file in 3 minutes, with a quality score of 71. A team member claims that only Method P combined fast processing with high quality.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support the team member's claim?
opts: Method P produced the highest quality score of the three methods, 92 out of 100.
Method R produced the smallest file, 22 megabytes, but took 3 minutes to do so.
Method P finished in 2 minutes with a quality score of 92, whereas Method Q scored 90 but took 8 minutes and Method R took 3 minutes but scored only 71.
Methods P and Q both earned quality scores above 90 out of 100.
why: Choice C shows P is fast and high quality, while each rival fails on one of the two measures. Choice D mentions quality only, so it cannot show that P alone is also fast.

passage: On Marek Island, the weather is so ______ that fishermen pack both sunscreen and raincoats every morning, because a clear sky can turn stormy within an hour.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: unpredictable
constant
mild
seasonal
why: A clear sky turning stormy within an hour shows the weather cannot be predicted, so 'unpredictable' is correct. 'Constant' contradicts the sudden change described.

passage: After months of daily practice, Lena played the difficult piano piece so ______ that the audience forgot it was a student recital and listened as though a professional were on stage.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: clumsily
skillfully
nervously
reluctantly
why: The audience treated her like a professional, so she played 'skillfully'. 'Clumsily' would not make listeners forget it was a student recital.

passage: Because the desert receives very little rain, the plants that live there have adapted to ______ water, storing it in thick stems and leaves for the long dry periods.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: waste
ignore
conserve
pollute
why: Storing water in stems and leaves is a way of saving it, so 'conserve' fits. 'Waste' is the opposite of what storing water for dry periods achieves.

passage: Over the years, the detective's ______ attention to detail meant that even a single misplaced button or a faint footprint in the dust did not escape her notice.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: careless
brief
indifferent
meticulous
why: Noticing tiny clues shows extremely careful attention, so 'meticulous' is correct. 'Careless' and 'indifferent' describe the opposite of noticing small details.

passage: Mara was ______ about the school trip to the science museum; she had packed her bag the night before and could hardly sleep because she was looking forward to it so much.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: eager
doubtful
bored
fearful
why: Packing early and being unable to sleep from excitement show she was 'eager'. 'Doubtful' and 'fearful' do not match the strong anticipation described.

passage: The village's old stone bridge has survived floods, storms, and nearly three centuries of heavy use, which is a sign of how ______ its builders' work was.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: fragile
durable
hasty
ordinary
why: Surviving three centuries of floods and use shows the bridge was built to last, so 'durable' fits. 'Fragile' means easily broken, the opposite of the evidence.

passage: Unlike her talkative older brother, Priya was ______, often sitting through an entire family dinner without saying more than a few words to anyone.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: boastful
cheerful
reserved
generous
why: The contrast with a talkative brother and the few words spoken point to someone quiet and 'reserved'. 'Boastful' would describe someone who talks a lot about themselves.

passage: The old map was so ______ that the hikers could not tell which of the three trails led to the lake, because the lines were smudged and most of the labels had faded.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: detailed
colorful
accurate
unclear
why: Smudged lines and faded labels make a map hard to read, so 'unclear' is correct. 'Detailed' and 'accurate' would let the hikers choose a trail.

passage: Botanist Ines Varga found that the moss grew ______ on the north side of the rocks, where shade kept the surface damp, but only sparsely on the drier, sunny south side.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: abundantly
accidentally
temporarily
gradually
why: The word 'but only sparsely' sets up a contrast, so the north side must have had plentiful moss, which 'abundantly' conveys. 'Gradually' describes speed, not the contrast in amount.

passage: The economist's forecast was deliberately ______: rather than predicting a specific figure, she said only that prices would probably rise somewhat, depending on how the harvest went.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: emphatic
noncommittal
mistaken
ambitious
why: Avoiding a specific figure and hedging with 'probably' and 'somewhat' is 'noncommittal'. 'Emphatic' means forceful and certain, which the hedged forecast is not.

passage: Early photographers needed their subjects to hold perfectly still for several seconds, so portraits from the 1840s rarely show smiles; the stiff expressions were not a matter of mood but a ______ of the technology.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: denial
mixture
consequence
preference
why: The stiff faces resulted from the long exposure time, so they were a 'consequence' of the technology. 'Preference' suggests people chose not to smile, which the passage rules out.

passage: Although the new stadium's design was widely praised as ______, its roof leaked during the first heavy rainstorm, which embarrassed the architects who had promised a flawless building.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: dull
ordinary
flawed
innovative
why: 'Although' signals a contrast with the leaking roof, so the design must have been praised positively as 'innovative'. 'Flawed' would not contrast with the leak.

passage: Dr. Okafor's lecture on ocean tides was remarkably ______ to beginners: she defined every technical term, used simple diagrams, and paused often to ask whether anyone in the room was lost.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: accessible
exclusive
ambiguous
restrictive
why: Defining terms and checking understanding made the lecture easy for newcomers to follow, so 'accessible' fits. 'Exclusive' would mean it shut beginners out.

passage: The arctic fox's coat changes with the seasons, turning white in winter and brown in summer, an ______ that helps the animal blend into its surroundings throughout the year.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: accident
adaptation
obstacle
illusion
why: A seasonal change that helps an animal survive is an 'adaptation'. 'Accident' suggests chance, but the passage describes a regular, useful pattern.

passage: The two neighbors had argued for years over the garden fence, but a shared storm cleanup ______ their relationship, and by autumn they were trading tomatoes and gossip over that same fence.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: ended
ignored
softened
tested
why: Trading tomatoes and gossip shows the relationship became friendlier, so the cleanup 'softened' it. 'Tested' does not explain the friendly outcome.

passage: Critics described the novelist's early work as ______, filled with elaborate sentences and ornate imagery, while her later books used plain language and short chapters.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: sparse
humble
blunt
florid
why: Elaborate sentences and ornate imagery describe an overly decorated style, which 'florid' means. 'Sparse' and 'blunt' describe the plain style of her later books.

passage: A good chart maker must be ______ about scale: even a small error in measuring distance, repeated across a whole sea chart, can send a ship miles off course.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: exacting
relaxed
hopeful
indifferent
why: Because small errors grow into large ones, the maker must demand precision, which 'exacting' means. 'Relaxed' and 'indifferent' would invite the errors the passage warns about.

passage: The museum's new director is known for being ______, willing to try unusual exhibits, such as one built entirely from recycled kitchen appliances, that more cautious curators would have rejected.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: conventional
adventurous
thrifty
secretive
why: Trying unusual ideas that cautious curators would refuse shows a willingness to take risks, so 'adventurous' fits. 'Conventional' is the opposite, meaning she follows tradition.

passage: Though the festival director's remarks seemed ______ to the audience, offering warm praise to every sponsor in the room, those who read the transcript later noticed that she had promised nothing at all.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: evasive
hostile
gracious
hesitant
why: Warm praise for every sponsor would seem 'gracious' on the surface, and the contrast with the empty promises is the point. 'Evasive' is what the later readers might say, but it does not fit how the remarks seemed while she was offering praise.

passage: The archivist's catalog proved more ______ than its critics expected: although it covered thousands of letters, it contained no obvious omissions or duplicate entries, and any item could be found within minutes.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: ambitious
tedious
selective
thorough
why: No omissions and quick retrieval describe a catalog that is complete and careful, so 'thorough' fits. 'Selective' contradicts the lack of omissions, and 'ambitious' describes the goal rather than the result the passage reports.

passage: Because later observations only ______ confirmed the physicist's predictions about the comet's path, with a few measurements still disagreeing, she declined to claim certainty about where it would pass.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: partially
conclusively
hastily
repeatedly
why: Some measurements still disagreed, so the confirmation was incomplete, which 'partially' conveys. 'Conclusively' would justify certainty, and 'repeatedly' says nothing about the disagreeing measurements.

passage: The composer's final symphony is often called ______: rather than building toward a triumphant ending, it fades into a quiet passage that seems to leave its central question unanswered.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: bombastic
inconclusive
jubilant
repetitive
why: An ending that fades and leaves the main question unanswered is 'inconclusive'. 'Jubilant' and 'bombastic' describe the loud, triumphant ending the passage says the piece avoids.

passage: In the village's oral tradition, the great flood grows more ______ with each retelling: the water rises a little higher, the night lasts a little longer, and the single boat that was saved becomes three.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: reliable
plausible
embellished
subdued
why: Details that grow bigger at each retelling show the story is being 'embellished'. 'Plausible' is wrong because added exaggeration makes a tale less believable, not more.

passage: The negotiator's reputation rested on her ability to be ______ without seeming weak: she could concede a minor point graciously while holding firmly to the issues that mattered most.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: obstinate
impulsive
indulgent
flexible
why: Giving way on small points while staying firm on key ones is being 'flexible'. 'Indulgent' means overly lenient, which would make her seem weak rather than avoid it.

passage: After a decade studying coastal erosion, geologist Tomas Reyes had grown ______ the idea that any shoreline could be permanently protected; he argued instead that communities should plan for the sea to keep advancing.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
opts: enthusiastic about
skeptical of
indifferent to
puzzled by
why: He argues that communities should plan for the sea to advance, which shows he doubts permanent protection is possible, so 'skeptical of' fits. 'Indifferent to' does not fit because he argues actively about the subject.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: The island of Karvel has no trees taller than a person, because the wind off the northern sea never rests. Farmers there build low stone walls around their potato fields, and the walls break the wind enough for the crops to grow. Visitors often assume the walls are meant to keep animals out, but their real job is to shelter the plants from the weather.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
opts: To describe the different crops that are grown on Karvel
To clarify what the stone walls on Karvel are actually used for
To argue that visitors should avoid the island's windy coast
To compare farming on Karvel with farming on other islands
why: The text ends by correcting the visitors' assumption and stating the walls' real job, which is sheltering plants from wind. Choice A is wrong because crops are only mentioned in passing, and no comparison or advice to visitors appears.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: Dr. Selva Iyer argues that the old clock tower in the town square should be torn down because it no longer keeps accurate time.
Text 2: The tower's clock does run slow, but the building is the oldest in town and a favorite meeting place. Rather than demolish it, the council should hire someone to repair the clock.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Dr. Iyer's argument in Text 1?
opts: By agreeing that the tower should be removed but suggesting a later date
By proving that the tower's clock actually keeps accurate time
By claiming that the tower is too unsafe to repair
By accepting that the clock has a problem while rejecting demolition as the remedy
why: Text 2 admits the clock runs slow, which concedes Text 1's problem, but proposes repair instead of demolition. Choice B is wrong because Text 2 says the clock does run slow.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: Bees communicate through movement. When a forager finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a figure-eight pattern known as the waggle dance. The angle of the dance relative to vertical tells other bees the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. Nearby bees follow the dancer and then fly out to the patch.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence ("The angle of the dance ... to the sun") in the text as a whole?
opts: It explains how the dance carries specific information to other bees.
It introduces a view that the rest of the text disputes.
It gives historical background on how the dance was discovered.
It states the conclusion that the earlier sentences were building toward.
why: The sentence tells how the dance conveys direction, which develops the idea of communication through movement. Choice D is wrong because the passage continues past that sentence to describe what the other bees do next.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: Marine biologist Lena Okoro reports that reef fish in Sorrel Bay grew noticeably larger in the five years after fishing there was banned.
Text 2: A separate team, working in nearby Tindal Bay, measured fish before and after a similar fishing ban. They, too, recorded a clear increase in the average size of the fish.
stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between Text 1 and Text 2?
opts: Text 2 questions the method that Okoro used in Sorrel Bay.
Text 2 shows that fishing bans can harm reef fish.
Text 2 offers similar findings from another location that support Text 1.
Text 2 shifts the discussion to a different species of fish.
why: Both texts report larger fish after a ban, and Text 2's results come from a different bay, so they back up Text 1. Choice A is wrong because Text 2 never criticizes Okoro's method.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: When Tomas first took up the cello, his practice sessions sounded more like creaking doors than music, and his neighbors winced through the walls. After a year of daily lessons, however, he could play a simple melody cleanly. Today, those same neighbors sometimes stop on the stairs to listen.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
opts: It presents a problem and then argues that the problem cannot be solved.
It lists several instruments and compares how hard each is to learn.
It criticizes the neighbors for being unkind to a beginner.
It moves from an early struggle to later improvement and a changed reaction.
why: The text begins with Tomas's poor playing, shows his progress, and ends with the neighbors listening willingly. Choice A is wrong because the difficulty is overcome, not shown to be unsolvable.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: Many people believe that a goldfish remembers things for only about three seconds, so a goldfish bowl is supposed to be a new place every moment.
Text 2: In a school experiment, goldfish learned to press a small lever to get food. When the lever was returned after several weeks, the fish went straight to it and pressed it.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?
opts: The belief is contradicted by evidence that goldfish can remember for weeks.
The belief is correct but applies only to goldfish raised in school tanks.
The belief cannot be tested because goldfish cannot be trained.
The belief is supported because goldfish need food to be reminded of the lever.
why: Fish that return to a lever after several weeks plainly remember for far longer than three seconds, so Text 2 undercuts Text 1. Choice B is wrong because nothing in Text 2 limits the result to school tanks.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: Every Saturday, the square in front of Dunmore Hall fills with stalls. Farmers sell apples and cheese, a baker sells rye loaves, and a retired teacher sells secondhand books for a few coins. By noon the square is crowded, and by evening only a few paper bags blowing across the stones remain.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
opts: To argue that the market should be moved away from the square
To explain the method a baker uses to make rye bread
To describe how a place changes over the course of a market day
To compare what farmers earn with what the teacher earns
why: The text moves from stalls filling the square to a crowd at noon to emptiness at evening, so it describes change across a day. Choice B is wrong because the baker is only one item in a list of sellers.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: Principal Hana Ito says that the new solar panels on the school roof will cut the school's electricity bill by about a quarter each year.
Text 2: A parent responds that the panels are a good idea but were expensive to buy and install, so the school may not see any real savings for many years.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Principal Ito's claim?
opts: By rejecting the panels as a poor idea that should be removed
By acknowledging the benefit while raising a concern about the cost
By proposing that the school switch to a cheaper form of energy
By confirming that savings will begin immediately

stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
opts: It introduces a researcher's study, reports what she observed, and then gives her conclusion.
It states a general theory and then offers two examples that disprove it.
It compares two towns and recommends which one other towns should copy.
It traces the factory's history and predicts when the town will recover.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critic's judgment in Text 1?
opts: By agreeing that the late works are inferior but explaining why
By arguing that the critic's standard overlooks the artist's purposes
By claiming that the early works were poorly received by the public
By recommending that the late works be hung beside the early works

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: Ines had packed the lantern carefully, wrapped in a wool scarf, though she doubted the climb would last past dusk. stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence ("The guide had promised ... another ridge") in the text as a whole?
opts: It describes the design of the lantern in detail.
It reveals that the guide deliberately misled Ines.
It shows that Ines is an experienced climber.
It shows the climb taking longer than expected, which sets up the need for the lantern.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Vale's proposal in Text 1?

By questioning it because the observed pattern does not fit what the proposal predicts

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: The first measures of the piece are nearly silent, played by a single violin. Slowly, other instruments join, one by one, until the full orchestra swells into a thunderous chord. stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
opts: To argue that the violin is the most important instrument in an orchestra
To describe how a piece of music builds and the effect its composer intended at the end
To criticize Whitfield's piece for beginning too quietly
To teach readers how an orchestra plays a loud chord

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:

By proposing that the bike lanes be built on a different street
By agreeing that bike lanes are useful but arguing they will work only with another change
By showing that more residents already cycle than Bell believes

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: Octopuses were long thought to be solitary and simple animals. Yet in a series of tests at the Pell Marine Institute, they unscrewed jar lids to reach food, and some even seemed to recognize individual keepers by sight. stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
opts: It presents an older assumption that the rest of the text goes on to complicate.
It gives evidence from the Pell Marine Institute tests.
It names the people who carried out the research.
It defines a technical term used later in the text.
why: The first sentence states the old view, and the later sentences give results that challenge it. Choice B is wrong because the Pell tests are introduced only in the second sentence.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: A local author writes that the village of Ashby was founded in 1420, citing a land deed dated that year that mentions the village by name.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
opts: By agreeing and adding a second deed from the same year
By arguing that Ashby is a full century older than 1420
By arguing that the deed proves less than Text 1 claims
By claiming that no deed can ever be used as historical evidence

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: In the final lap of the Brindle Cup, Aisha Verma was running third. Instead of sprinting at once, she held her pace and let the two leaders battle for the inside lane. stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?
opts: It offers an explanation that challenges the commentators' view of the race.
It introduces a new competitor who joins the race.
It lists the final standings of the Brindle Cup.
It criticizes the coach for relying on a risky plan.
why: The sentence contrasts the commentators' idea of luck with the coach's long training, giving a different explanation for the win. Choice C is wrong because no standings are listed beyond Aisha passing both leaders.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: A linguist argues that young children learn to speak best when adults talk to them directly, and that hearing speech from a television does little to help.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the linguist's argument in Text 1?
opts: By arguing that television is the best way to teach speech
By confirming that adult speech is the only source of language learning
By claiming that children learn language more slowly in villages
By suggesting that the emphasis on adult speech overlooks other important sources of learning
why: The Oru children learned fluently with little adult talk, so Text 2 implies that play with other children also matters. Choice B is wrong because the Oru results show adult speech is not the only source.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: Historians often describe the medieval fair at Wendover as a place of commerce, and the ledgers certainly show wool and salt changing hands. But the same ledgers record payments to jugglers, a bear keeper, and a minstrel who appeared year after year. Such entries suggest that merchants and townspeople attended not only to trade but to be entertained, and that the fair's commerce depended in part on its ability to draw a crowd.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
opts: It describes a common view and then dismisses it as entirely false.
It gives a year-by-year account of how the fair grew.
It acknowledges a conventional view, adds further evidence, and draws an inference that qualifies the view.
It contrasts the accounts of two historians who disagree about the ledgers.
why: The text grants that the ledgers show trade, then points to payments for entertainers, and infers that the fair's trade relied on entertainment. Choice A is wrong because the text says the ledgers certainly show commerce, so it does not call the view entirely false.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage:
Text 1: Ecologist Mara Quill argues that bringing the ash fox, a hunting animal, back to Tern Valley will reduce overgrazing, because deer will stay out of open meadows where they can be seen.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Quill's argument in Text 1?
opts: By denying that ash foxes change the behavior of deer at all
By accepting that the animals change deer behavior but doubting that the effect is lasting
By arguing that bringing back ash foxes would harm other species in the valley
By supporting Quill with evidence that the effect on deer is permanent
why: Text 2 calls the mechanism plausible and notes the early avoidance, but says the deer returned within a year, so it questions durability. Choice A is wrong because Text 2 says deer did avoid meadows at first.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: For years, Oskar kept his grandfather's pocket watch in a drawer, convinced that its broken spring made it worthless. When a watchmaker finally opened the case, she found, tucked behind the dial, a folded slip of paper bearing a single line of handwriting: the name of a village Oskar had never heard of. The watch still did not run, but Oskar no longer thought of it as broken; he thought of it as unfinished.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?
opts: It confirms that the watch was worthless after all.
It explains how the watchmaker repaired the broken spring.
It reveals what the slip of paper said.
It shows a change in Oskar's view of the watch, from a useless object to one with unresolved meaning.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Sandhu's argument in Text 1?

By denying that prices of handmade ceramics have risen
By agreeing that buyers value craftsmanship and adding that potters should charge more
By arguing that buyers no longer value handmade goods at all

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: A common explanation for why the lakes of the Calder Basin freeze later each winter is simple warming. If Aldous is right, the later freezing reflects a shift in how heat moves within the lakes rather than a warmer climate alone.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
opts: To prove that winter air temperatures in the Calder Basin have not changed
To compare Aldous's research with the work of several other hydrologists
To present a proposed explanation that challenges a common one for a puzzling change
To argue that lakes everywhere are freezing later than they used to
why: The text lays out the usual explanation, notes a problem with it, and introduces Aldous's alternative. Choice A is wrong because the text says only that air temperatures changed little and uses that to question one explanation.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the poet's claim in Text 1?
opts: By rejecting it on the grounds that rhyme is as common in poetry as ever
By agreeing that readers find rhyme childish and so poets should avoid it
By arguing that songs have replaced poetry as the main place readers look for verse
By granting that rhyme has become rarer in poetry while offering a different cause
why: Text 2 concedes the decline of rhyme in poetry but attributes it to poets rather than to readers' dislike. Choice A is wrong because Text 2 says rhyme has certainly become rarer in published poetry.

skill: Text Structure and Purpose, and Cross-Text Connections
passage: In his notebook, the naturalist Ferdinand Lacey recorded the arrival of swallows each spring for thirty years. Only in the last decade do the notes lengthen, mixing observation with remarks on the weather, on his failing knees, on the view from his window. The earlier entries give us the swallows; the later ones give us Lacey.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?
opts: It summarizes the data Lacey collected about the swallows.
It contrasts what the early and late entries reveal, sharpening the change the text has described.
It criticizes Lacey for neglecting science in his later years.
It introduces new evidence about when swallows migrate.
why: The sentence sums up the shift from bare records of birds to personal reflections, which the previous sentences have laid out. Choice A is wrong because the sentence says the later entries reveal Lacey himself, not more bird data.

The Salt Orchard won a regional prize for fiction in 2009.
Ilse Varden wrote a book that was published in 2009 and won a prize.

Students recalled many words from a list after sleeping.

Pell's weekly market, which opened in 1952 at a single corner, now fills three streets with 60 stalls.

The gills of an octopus receive blood from two hearts.

Odalys Fenn painted thirty canvases in the 1890s.

The Marenth lighthouse was built in 1790.
An electronic beacon replaced the Marenth lighthouse in 1990.

Volunteers either sat or walked while memorizing a list of words.
Volunteers who walked recalled an average of 14 words, compared with 11 words for volunteers who sat.

In a three-year study, hives near wildflower meadows produced 22 percent more honey than hives near farmland.
